title: Input and conversion
summary: Read what the user types, and turn text into numbers safely.

steps.title: Reading a line
body: `Console.ReadLine()` waits for the user to type a line and press Enter, then hands you that line as a `string`.
```csharp
Console.WriteLine("What is your name?");
string name = Console.ReadLine();
Console.WriteLine($"Hello, {name}!");
In the dojo, the **Input given** box under your program shows what was typed for you when you press Run.

> **Tip:** You may see a warning that `ReadLine()` could return `null` (no input at all). It is safe to ignore for now. Later starters write `Console.ReadLine()!` instead: the `!` tells the compiler *trust me, this is not null* and silences the warning. The nullability lesson explains it properly.

steps.title: Greeter
prompt: Read one line (a name) and print a greeting.
hints: Use string interpolation: a `$` before the quote and `{name}` inside.
Do not forget the comma, the space and the `!`.

steps.title: Input is always text
body: Even when the user types `42`, `ReadLine()` gives you the *string* `"42"`. You cannot do maths with it until you convert it.
```csharp
string text = Console.ReadLine();   // "42"
int number = int.Parse(text);       // 42
Console.WriteLine(number + 1);      // 43
`int.Parse` reads a whole number out of a string. `double.Parse` does the same for decimals.
Going the other way, every value has `.ToString()`: `42.ToString()` is `"42"`.

steps.prompt: The user types `5`. What does this print?
steps.explain: `input` is the string `"5"`, so `+` joins it to itself. After parsing, `+` adds numbers.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into a program that reads a number and prints its double.
steps.explain: Each line needs the variable created by the line before it: read, convert, calculate, print.

steps.title: When the text is not a number
body: `int.Parse("hello")` cannot succeed, so the program **crashes** with a `FormatException`. Users type nonsense all the time, so C# offers a safe version:
```csharp
string text = Console.ReadLine();
bool ok = int.TryParse(text, out int number);
Console.WriteLine(ok);       // True if it was a number
Console.WriteLine(number);   // the number, or 0 if it was not
`TryParse` never crashes. It answers `true` or `false`, and puts the converted value in the variable after `out`. If the text was not a number, that variable is `0`.

steps.explain: `int.Parse` refuses anything that is not a whole number, including `"1.5"`. `TryParse` reports the same failures as `false` instead of crashing.
`TryParse` returns a `bool` and delivers the number through the `out` variable.

steps.title: Fix the adder
steps.prompt: This program reads two numbers and should print their sum. For the input `2` and `3` it prints `23`. Fix it so it prints `5`.
hints: `a` and `b` are strings, so `+` is joining text.
Convert each one with `int.Parse(...)` before adding.

steps.title: Rectangle
prompt: Read a width and a height (two lines, whole numbers). Print the area and the perimeter in this format.
starter: // read the width and the height, then print the area and perimeter
hints: You can convert as you read: `int width = int.Parse(Console.ReadLine());`
Area is width times height. Perimeter is twice the sum of both.
Calculations can go inside interpolation braces: `{width * height}`.
